title: Create Sorted Array through Instructions
description: Brute force to optimized: replacing a physically shifted sorted array with a value-indexed Fenwick tree for fast smaller/greater counts.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array instructions, you insert its values one at a time into a growing array named "nums", always keeping nums sorted (using an insertion-sort style process). The cost of inserting instructions[i] is the MINIMUM of (the count of already-placed elements strictly less than it) and (the count of already-placed elements strictly greater than it). Return the total cost of all insertions, modulo 10^9 + 7.

blocks.text: Process instructions one value at a time. Before adding each value to the growing sorted collection, count how many already-placed values are smaller and how many are larger, add the smaller of those two counts to a running total, then add the current value to the collection.

blocks.title: Analogy: Sorting Playing Cards into Your Hand
blocks.text: Picture picking up cards one at a time and inserting each into a sorted hand. Each time, you glance at how many cards in your hand so far are lower, and how many are higher, and jot down whichever count is smaller before sliding the new card into place.

blocks.caption: For each new value, count smaller and larger already-placed values, and add the smaller count

blocks.text: Total cost is 1. Insert 1 (cost 0, nothing placed yet), insert 5 (cost 0, one smaller, zero larger), insert 6 (cost 0, two smaller, zero larger), insert 2 (cost 1, one smaller [the 1], two larger [5 and 6], min is 1).

Before jumping to any structure, notice the calculation needed at each step is exactly a "how many placed values are less than X" and "how many are greater than X" query, repeated after every insertion, which is the signature of a Fenwick tree over the value range.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A naive approach could maintain an actual sorted array and binary-search for the insertion point each time, then count directly from that point, correct, but each insertion into an array costs O(n) to shift elements.

Observation 2: What is actually needed is just COUNTS, not the physical sorted array itself: count of already-placed values less than x, and count of already-placed values greater than x.

Observation 3: A Fenwick tree indexed by VALUE (from 1 to the maximum instruction value) can answer "how many values <= x have been placed so far" via a prefix-sum query in O(log maxV), and can register a new placement in O(log maxV) as well.

Observation 4: less = prefix(x-1); greater = (number of elements placed before this one) - prefix(x) (values placed so far that are NOT <= x); add min(less, greater) to the running cost, then mark x as placed.
This leads to a Fenwick tree indexed by value, giving O(log maxV) per insertion for both the count query and the update, instead of O(n) per insertion with a physically shifted sorted array.
Maintain an actual sorted list. For each new value, binary-search for its insertion point, count smaller/larger directly from that point, then insert it (shifting elements).

items: Maintain a sorted list of values placed so far.
For each new value x, binary-search for the insertion index.
The insertion index directly gives the count of smaller values; count of larger values is (list length - insertion index for the rightmost equal position).
Add the minimum of these two counts to the total cost, then insert x into the sorted list.

codes.python:
import bisect

def create_sorted_array(instructions):
    MOD = 10**9 + 7
    sorted_list = []
    cost = 0
    for x in instructions:
        less = bisect.bisect_left(sorted_list, x)          # count strictly smaller
        greater = len(sorted_list) - bisect.bisect_right(sorted_list, x)  # count strictly greater
        cost += min(less, greater)
        sorted_list.insert(less, x)                          # O(n) shift
    return cost % MOD

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Binary search quickly finds where a value would fit, but the actual insertion into the array still costs O(n) because later elements must shift.
This is correct, but degrades to O(n squared) overall when many insertions happen.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case, O(log n) search but O(n) shift per insertion.
Space: O(n) for the sorted list.

Limitation: the physical array shift on every insertion is unnecessary; only COUNTS of smaller/larger values are needed, and a Fenwick tree can maintain and query those counts directly without ever physically shifting anything.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the physical array is unnecessary: the cost only depends on counts, never on the actual sorted order of the underlying values.

What a Fenwick tree gives instead: for value range 1 to maxV, treat the Fenwick tree as a frequency array where index x is incremented once x is placed; a prefix-sum query up to x directly gives "how many placed values are <= x" in O(log maxV).

How to get "less than x" and "greater than x": less = prefix(x - 1); greater = (elements placed so far) - prefix(x).

The core idea: index the Fenwick tree by VALUE, not by array position, since the "value seen so far" frequency is exactly what needs querying and updating.

Build a Fenwick tree sized to the maximum instruction value. For each instruction x, query prefix(x-1) for the smaller count and derive the greater count from the running insertion index, add the minimum to the total, then update the Fenwick tree at position x.

blocks.caption: A Fenwick tree over the value range answers smaller/greater counts in O(log maxV) per insertion

codes.python:
def create_sorted_array(instructions):
    MOD = 10**9 + 7
    max_v = max(instructions)
    bit = [0] * (max_v + 2)

    def update(i, delta):
        i += 1
        while i <= max_v + 1:
            bit[i] += delta
            i += i & (-i)

    def prefix(i):
        i += 1
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += bit[i]
            i -= i & (-i)
        return s

    cost = 0
    for idx, x in enumerate(instructions):
        less = prefix(x - 1)
        greater = idx - prefix(x)          # placed so far minus (<= x)
        cost += min(less, greater)
        update(x, 1)
    return cost % MOD

blocks.text: The Fenwick tree, indexed directly by value, maintains a running frequency count of every placed value. A prefix-sum query up to x-1 gives exactly the count of already-placed values strictly less than x, and subtracting prefix(x) from the running insertion index (the total number placed so far) gives exactly the count strictly greater than x, since prefix(x) counts everything placed so far that is <= x.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log maxV), one Fenwick query and one Fenwick update per element.
Space: O(maxV) for the Fenwick tree array.

items: Forgetting to subtract prefix(x) (not prefix(x-1)) when computing the "greater than" count, causing off-by-one errors.
Not applying modulo arithmetic correctly on the running cost, given up to 10^5 insertions each contributing up to 10^5 to the cost.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "the cost formula only needs counts, so a Fenwick tree indexed by value replaces the need for a physically maintained sorted array" is the key insight to lead with.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid shifting the array on every insertion", think: Fenwick tree indexed by value, prefix sums give the counts directly.

Reverse Pairs and other "counting inversions" problems, all solvable with a Fenwick tree over value or rank.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force with a physically shifted sorted array runs in O(n squared) worst case; the Fenwick-tree solution runs in O(n log maxV) time and O(maxV) space.

items: Pattern: Fenwick tree indexed by value, replacing a physically maintained sorted structure.
Core Idea: track a running frequency count of placed values; use prefix sums to get counts of smaller and greater values in O(log maxV).
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n log maxV) for the optimized Fenwick tree approach.
Most Important Observation: only counts are needed, never the actual sorted array, so a value-indexed Fenwick tree suffices.
Interview Difficulty: a standard, well-recognized application of Fenwick trees for counting.
One line memory trick: count smaller and greater with a value-indexed Fenwick tree, add the smaller count.
